t.2.52.1: When the king had recovered his breath and come back again from his swoon, he summoned that charioteer for the sake of the news of Rāma.
t.2.52.2: The aged one, deeply tormented like a newly captured elephant, sighing heavily and brooding, like an elephant that is unwell.
t.2.52.3: But the king, like one gravely afflicted, spoke to the charioteer, who had come before him, his limbs covered with dust, his face full of tears, and downcast.
t.2.52.4: Where now will the righteous-souled one dwell, taking shelter at the foot of a tree? What will Rāghava, who has known only the utmost comfort, eat, O charioteer? How does the son of the lord of the earth lie upon the bare ground like one who has no protector?
t.2.52.5: How will Rāma, whom foot-soldiers, chariots and elephants used to follow as he went forth, live now that he has taken refuge in the desolate forest?
t.2.52.6: How have the two princes, together with Vaidehī, reached the forest, roamed by fierce beasts and wild animals and haunted by black serpents?
t.2.52.7: O Sumantra, how did the two princes, having got down from the chariot, go on foot together with the delicate and pitiable Sītā?
t.2.52.8: Truly you have attained your purpose, O charioteer, you by whom my two sons were seen entering the depths of the forest, like the two Aśvins entering Mandara.
t.2.52.10: Thus urged by the lord of men, the charioteer spoke to the king in a faltering voice, a voice choked and gripped by tears.
t.2.52.9: Sumantra, on reaching the forest, what words did Rāma speak, what did Lakṣmaṇa say, and what did Maithilī say? Tell me, charioteer, how Rāma sat, how he slept, and what he ate.
t.2.52.11: O great king, Rāghava, ever upholding dharma, joined his palms in reverence, bowed low with his head, and said to me:
t.2.52.12: O charioteer, on my word, the feet of that great-souled father of mine, the self-realized one who is worthy of reverence, are to be saluted with your head bowed.
t.2.52.13: O Sūta, on my word you must address the whole inner palace, conveying to all without distinction my wishes for their good health, and my salutations to each as befits them.
t.2.52.14: And to my mother Kausalyā convey my well-being and my salutation, saying: 'O queen, tend the feet of the king as you would a god's.'
t.2.52.16: And the mighty-armed one, the joy of the Ikṣvāku race, should be told: "Established as heir-apparent, obey and support your father, who is established in the kingship."
t.2.52.15: Bharata is to be told of our well-being, and told also in my words: 'Conduct yourself toward all the mothers alike, in the proper and fitting manner.'
t.2.52.17: O great king, even as he was speaking to me thus, the greatly renowned Rāma, his eyes coppery-red like lotuses, shed tears profusely.
t.2.52.18: But Lakṣmaṇa, greatly enraged and sighing heavily, spoke these words: "For what offense has this prince been banished?"
t.2.52.19: If Rāma has been sent into exile, whether it was brought about by greed or on account of the granting of a boon, in every way a wicked deed has been done. But I see no reason at all for the abandonment of Rāma.
t.2.52.21: For my part, I do not perceive any fatherhood in the great king; Rāghava is my brother, my master, my kinsman and my father.
t.2.52.20: The banishment of Rāghava, undertaken without reflection and contrary to what is right, out of shallowness of mind, will give rise to a great outcry.
t.2.52.22: Having cast off him who is dear to all the world and devoted to the welfare of all the world, how could the whole world remain devoted to you after this deed?
t.2.52.23: But Jānakī, O great king, the poor suffering lady, stood there sighing, motionless and forgetful of herself, as though her mind had been struck by a spirit.
t.2.52.24: The illustrious princess, who had never before known misfortune, weeping with that grief, said nothing at all to me.
t.2.52.25: Gazing up at her husband with a face that was withering, she suddenly let her tears fall when she saw me departing.
t.2.52.26: Just so Rāma stood, his face wet with tears and his hands joined in reverence, guarded by the arms of Lakṣmaṇa; and just so the unhappy Sītā, weeping, gazes after the royal chariot and after me.
